title: Final self-assessment — 40 questions across Modules 1–8
body_md:
## Final self-assessment: decisions, not labels

This untimed, not proctored self-assessment has **40 questions, five from each of Modules 1–8**. Each asks what you would infer or do in a concrete situation. Some messages are plausible and legitimate; spotting pressure is a cue to verify, not proof of a crime. Read why every choice works or fails before moving on.

Choose one answer per question. The personal benchmark is **80% (32 of 40)**. You can retake the complete set. A pass is stored in this browser for the local completion record. With optional progress sync, an encrypted copy can be stored remotely. The result is **not independently verified**, server-issued, or a measure of real-world competence. There is no timer or external assessor. A previous local pass may remain in the browser after a weaker retake, so use the new score for honest self-reflection.

### How to review

Afterward, revisit questions you missed by **decision type**: reading evidence and report denominators (Module 1); pressure and independent contact (2); destination and login route (3); password, MFA and recovery (4); payment and provider response (5); voice, video and provenance (6); device, browser and network limits (7); containment, evidence and recovery (8). Write one practical change for your own setup. Do not enter real passwords, codes, messages, URLs or payment details here.

### Source scope

These scenarios are synthetic. The [UK NCSC scam guide](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/phishing-scams/spot-scams), [NIST authenticator standard](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/authenticators/), [FTC post-scam guidance](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/what-do-if-you-were-scammed), and [C2PA provenance guidance](https://spec.c2pa.org/specifications/specifications/2.4/security/Harms_Modelling.html) were checked on 2026-10-20. UK NCSC advice on breaking contact, NIST authenticator distinctions, FTC US consumer payment/recovery guidance, and C2PA provenance limits inform the questions. Reporting and payment rights depend on your country and provider; no source certifies this assessment.

questions.question: A report says “10,000 scam complaints last year.” What can you conclude from that figure?

choices.text: The reporting system received 10,000 complaints; it does not by itself measure all victimization.
choices.explanation: Reports have a reporting denominator and may be unverified.

choices.text: Exactly 10,000 people were scammed.
choices.explanation: One person may report more than once and many victims never report.

choices.text: The scam probability for any reader is 10,000 divided by the country population.
choices.explanation: A report count is not a population survey or individual probability.

questions.question: A message arrives through a channel you rarely use and includes little context. What should drive the first decision?

choices.text: Identify the requested action and verify a consequential claim through a known route.
choices.explanation: Channel alone does not diagnose fraud; the action and independent check matter.

choices.text: Treat every SMS as fraudulent.
choices.explanation: Legitimate services also send texts.

choices.text: Trust the message if it addresses you by name.
choices.explanation: Names are commonly available and do not prove sender control.

questions.question: A stranger builds a friendship, then introduces a private investing site. Which pattern warrants the closest check?

choices.text: A one-off shipping scam.
choices.explanation: No shipment or seller transaction appears in the scenario.

choices.text: A state-directed intelligence operation.
choices.explanation: Nothing here establishes a state actor.

choices.text: A relationship-based investment fraud pattern.
choices.explanation: Trust-building followed by a private investment invitation is the relevant pattern; it remains a reason to verify, not proof about this person.

choices.text: A routine account-recovery request.
choices.explanation: The requested action is investment, not account recovery.

questions.question: An attacker emails accounts payable while impersonating a CFO to redirect a transfer. What is this usually called?

choices.text: Ransomware
choices.explanation: Ransomware encrypts or extorts data; this is a payment-instruction impersonation.

choices.text: BEC (Business Email Compromise)
choices.explanation: BEC is the umbrella for executive-impersonation schemes that redirect payments.

choices.text: Quishing
choices.explanation: A QR lure is not described.

choices.text: Credential stuffing
choices.explanation: Credential stuffing uses reused credentials at login; it is not the payment instruction.

questions.question: A video meeting shows several familiar executives requesting a large transfer. What control is strongest?

choices.text: Pause and confirm the specific transaction through a separately held contact and normal approvals.
choices.explanation: The check works whether the video is fake or an account is compromised.

choices.text: Look for lip-sync errors and pay if none appear.
choices.explanation: Absence of artifacts does not authorize payment.

choices.text: Ask the same meeting chat to confirm in writing.
choices.explanation: The same potentially controlled channel can repeat the instruction.

questions.question: A ticket offer says “Only three left; decide in ten minutes.” What does this show?

choices.text: Scarcity and urgency are pressure cues; independently check the seller and terms before paying.
choices.explanation: Real limited inventory exists, so the cue calls for verification rather than a verdict.

choices.text: It proves the seller is fraudulent.
choices.explanation: A genuine sale can also be time-limited.

choices.text: It proves the seller is genuine because it shows stock data.
choices.explanation: The displayed count can be invented.

questions.question: How do you break a pretext in a suspicious call?

choices.text: Demand the caller's badge number.
choices.explanation: A badge number supplied by the same caller is not independent evidence.

choices.text: Hang up and call back on a number you already had.
choices.explanation: The pretext lives inside the channel; switching channels collapses it.

choices.text: Argue with the caller until they slip up.
choices.explanation: Arguing gives the caller more time to steer you.

choices.text: Stay on the line so police can trace it.
choices.explanation: Staying connected does not authenticate the caller or safely trace them.

questions.question: A caller asks you to move money to a “safe account” while staying on the line. Which detail most changes your response?

choices.text: The caller has a foreign accent.
choices.explanation: An accent is not evidence of fraud.

choices.text: The caller insists on staying on the line during a financial action.
choices.explanation: A caller-directed “safe account” transfer is the high-risk action; stop and verify through the bank independently.

choices.text: The caller knows the last four digits of your card.
choices.explanation: Knowledge of card digits does not authorize a new transfer.

choices.text: The call came outside business hours.
choices.explanation: Calls outside business hours can be legitimate.

questions.question: A stranger you've chatted with for weeks introduces a small crypto platform and helps you make a successful test withdrawal. The strongest indicator of pig-butchering is:

choices.text: The promised returns are unrealistic.
choices.explanation: High returns are also a warning, but the relationship-to-platform transition is the pattern asked about.

choices.text: The introduction came sideways from a stranger who built rapport for weeks.
choices.explanation: The combination of trust-building and investment referral is the warning; even a small successful withdrawal would not prove the platform safe.

choices.text: A relative of theirs supposedly works at the platform.
choices.explanation: A claimed relative at the platform is unverified social proof.

choices.text: They suggest starting small.
choices.explanation: A small starting amount can lower resistance without validating the site.

questions.question: Which phrase in a live call is sufficient on its own to end the conversation?

choices.text: 'For security, please install AnyDesk so I can clean your computer remotely.'
choices.explanation: An unsolicited caller directing you to install remote-access software creates an immediate access risk. End the call and verify support independently if needed.

choices.text: 'I'll send you the details by email.'
choices.explanation: Offering email details alone does not require ending every legitimate call.

choices.text: 'Could you confirm your name?'
choices.explanation: Asking a name alone can occur in normal service calls; avoid giving sensitive details to unverified callers.

choices.text: 'Sorry for the noise on my side.'
choices.explanation: Background noise alone is not a fraud signal.

questions.question: In the fictional URL `https://login.paypal.com.account-verify.example/signin`, which part names the site under the reserved .example suffix?

choices.text: paypal.com
choices.explanation: The visible paypal.com string is inside a different host.

choices.text: login.paypal.com
choices.explanation: This is only a prefix within a different host.

choices.text: account-verify.example
choices.explanation: The .example suffix is reserved for examples. In this fictional host, account-verify is the label immediately under it; paypal.com appears only in left-side labels. Real suffixes such as co.uk need different parsing.

choices.text: signin.example
choices.explanation: signin is in the path, not the host.

questions.question: A brand name appears in a URL with a visually similar character. What is the useful response?

choices.text: Use a saved entry point or type the known service address yourself, then inspect the real host.
choices.explanation: Lookalike characters make visual reading unreliable; an independent route helps.

choices.text: Assume every non-Latin character in a URL is malicious.
choices.explanation: Internationalized domain names can be legitimate.

choices.text: Trust the page if it has HTTPS.
choices.explanation: HTTPS protects the connection, not the identity of the business.

questions.question: A password manager does not autofill on a page that resembles your bank. What should you do?

choices.text: Assume the vault is broken and reset it immediately.
choices.explanation: A vault fault is possible, but resetting it before checking the address can create avoidable recovery work.

choices.text: Stop and open the bank by a saved or independently chosen route; inspect the address before entering credentials.
choices.explanation: Stop, inspect the actual address and open the bank via a saved or independently chosen route. Autofill failure is a useful warning, not proof of phishing.

choices.text: Paste the password manually because the bank probably changed its login flow.
choices.explanation: A real login change is possible, but manual paste into this unverified page bypasses the domain check.

choices.text: Ignore the warning because private browsing can block autofill.
choices.explanation: Private browsing may affect autofill, but it does not establish the site identity.

questions.question: At work, an email asks you to re-enter payroll credentials. You did not click it. What is the useful report?

choices.text: Use your organization’s established phishing-report route, keeping the message intact.
choices.explanation: The security team can inspect it; local procedures differ.

choices.text: Forward the live link to every colleague so they can test it.
choices.explanation: This spreads a potentially harmful link.

choices.text: Delete it silently; reporting has no value.
choices.explanation: A report can help protect other recipients.

questions.question: A poster next to the office copier displays a QR code and says 'Your Microsoft 365 password is expiring — scan to renew'. What's the safest move?

choices.text: Scan and renew — IT often posts these.
choices.explanation: IT may post notices, but the code itself is not an authenticated route.

choices.text: Renew through the company's official SSO portal that you already use, and report the poster to IT.
choices.explanation: Posted QR codes are not the right channel for credential changes — anyone with badge-in access could have put them up. Use the trusted SSO portal you already use, and warn IT.

choices.text: Ignore it — passwords don't expire anymore.
choices.explanation: Password-expiry rules depend on the organization; the poster still needs checking.

choices.text: Scan only if the URL preview looks plausible.
choices.explanation: A plausible preview can still lead to an attacker-controlled destination.

questions.question: A forum tells you your password was exposed. What is the most useful immediate account check?

choices.text: Change the password on the forum.
choices.explanation: The forum needs attention too, but checking reuse prevents the same secret from opening other accounts.

choices.text: Change the exposed password wherever reused, starting with important accounts, and secure the forum account.
choices.explanation: Change the exposed password wherever it was reused, prioritizing important accounts; also secure the forum account. If unique, focus on that account and watch for related exposure.

choices.text: Create a new email and migrate everything.
choices.explanation: Creating a new address does not remove the exposed password.

choices.text: Wait to see if your bank notifies you.
choices.explanation: Waiting for a bank notice leaves possible reuse unaddressed.

questions.question: Which MFA tier is phishing-resistant by protocol design?

choices.text: SMS one-time codes
choices.explanation: An SMS code can be relayed or intercepted.

choices.text: TOTP authenticator app
choices.explanation: An app-generated code can also be relayed to a phishing page.

choices.text: Hardware key / passkey (FIDO2)
choices.explanation: FIDO2 binds the signature to the origin URL — a fake page cannot produce a valid signature for the real domain.

choices.text: Email-link confirmation
choices.explanation: An email link is not generally origin-bound like FIDO2.

questions.question: You add a passkey for one account. What still needs attention?

choices.text: Check where that particular passkey is stored and which recovery methods remain enabled.
choices.explanation: Device-bound and synced credentials differ; recovery can remain a weaker route.

choices.text: All passkeys are stored in iCloud.
choices.explanation: Storage depends on platform, provider and account setup.

choices.text: A passkey makes account recovery irrelevant.
choices.explanation: Loss of access and recovery attacks still need planning.

questions.question: A work account uses an authenticator app, but its recovery phone number is no longer yours. What should you do?

choices.text: Update recovery through the service or administrator and add supported backup methods.
choices.explanation: The live recovery route is part of account security.

choices.text: Ignore the number because app codes protect all account routes.
choices.explanation: Recovery may bypass the sign-in factor.

choices.text: Send a colleague a screenshot of your backup codes.
choices.explanation: Backup codes are secrets and must be stored privately.

questions.question: A password manager flags reused and exposed passwords. Where should you start?

choices.text: Renaming your accounts to less guessable usernames.
choices.explanation: Changing usernames does not address a known reused secret.

choices.text: Fix flagged reused or exposed passwords, starting with important accounts.
choices.explanation: Fix flagged reused or exposed passwords, starting with important accounts, and review available MFA and recovery. Do not rotate every strong unique password on a calendar.

choices.text: Deleting all old emails.
choices.explanation: Deleting mail does not change account credentials.

choices.text: Adding a CAPTCHA to your home Wi-Fi.
choices.explanation: A home Wi-Fi CAPTCHA is not a remedy for reused passwords.

questions.question: An online store wants to charge you for a PS5 at 90% off MSRP via Bitcoin or gift cards, on a 14-day-old domain. Which signal is the *strongest* by itself?

choices.text: The domain age of 14 days.
choices.explanation: A new domain warrants a check but is not conclusive by itself.

choices.text: Payment options exclude major cards and use only non-reversible methods.
choices.explanation: Gift-card or crypto-only payment in this unfamiliar, steeply discounted store sharply reduces normal dispute options; verify the seller and choose a protected method if available.

choices.text: The 'only 3 left' urgency.
choices.explanation: Scarcity language is a pressure cue, not proof.

choices.text: The store name contains 'sony'.
choices.explanation: A brand word in the store name does not prove affiliation.

questions.question: After posting about a loss, you receive an unsolicited offer to “recover” your money for a fee. What now?

choices.text: Do not pay or share data; contact the original payment provider through its official route.
choices.explanation: Unexpected recovery offers can compound the loss, while provider options depend on payment method.

choices.text: Pay a small test fee to establish credibility.
choices.explanation: The fee can be the next loss; it proves no recovery ability.

choices.text: Send transaction and identity documents to the stranger first.
choices.explanation: This exposes more sensitive information without validating the service.

questions.question: A 'CFO' emails accounts payable asking to update a vendor's IBAN before the next invoice. Which control prevents the wire-redirection fraud?

choices.text: Verify the From-domain matches the vendor's real domain.
choices.explanation: A matching From domain can come from a compromised mailbox.

choices.text: Call the vendor's CFO on a phone number you already had and verbally confirm the IBAN change.
choices.explanation: Confirm the exact change through a previously recorded supplier contact and the normal second-approval process; the known contact need not be the CFO personally.

choices.text: Forward to IT for analysis before processing.
choices.explanation: IT analysis can help, but payment control still needs independent supplier confirmation.

choices.text: Check the IBAN format is country-valid.
choices.explanation: A formally valid account number can belong to the wrong recipient.

questions.question: Which payment-method combination defends best against both physical and digital card skimming?

choices.text: Memorising your number.
choices.explanation: Memorizing a card number does not protect it when used at a compromised terminal or site.

choices.text: Apple Pay / Google Pay where possible + virtual cards + real-time transaction alerts.
choices.explanation: Where supported, tokenized wallet payments and limited-use virtual cards can reduce card-number exposure; transaction alerts help detect misuse, not prevent it.

choices.text: Only shopping on stores you've never used before.
choices.explanation: Unfamiliar stores are not inherently safer.

choices.text: Avoiding online shopping entirely.
choices.explanation: Avoiding all online shopping does not address physical card exposure.

questions.question: You discover a bank transfer to a changed supplier account may be fraudulent. What is the first payment-response action?

choices.text: Contact the sending bank’s official fraud channel now and ask what recall, hold or trace is available.
choices.explanation: The bank needs early notice; options depend on transfer rail and jurisdiction.

choices.text: Wait for absolute proof before telling the bank.
choices.explanation: Delay may reduce available payment actions.

choices.text: Promise the supplier that the transfer will certainly be reversed.
choices.explanation: Reversal is not guaranteed.

questions.question: Which defensive strategy is *most durable* against improving generative-AI capabilities?

choices.text: Training to spot visual deepfake artifacts.
choices.explanation: Visible defects may disappear as tools improve.

choices.text: Out-of-band verification protocols (callback to known numbers, family code words).
choices.explanation: Independent contact and transaction approvals remain useful as synthetic media improves; a family word is only an extra signal, not sole proof.

choices.text: Avoiding any AI-generated content entirely.
choices.explanation: Avoiding all generated content is not a workable verification process.

choices.text: Trusting AI-text detector tools.
choices.explanation: A detector score cannot authenticate the speaker or authorize a payment.

questions.question: Someone sounds like your relative and urgently requests gift-card numbers. What check is best?

choices.text: End the call and reach the relative through a saved number or another trusted person.
choices.explanation: Voice can be cloned or imitated; a separately chosen route tests the story.

choices.text: Treat the voice as proof of identity.
choices.explanation: A familiar sound is not authentication.

choices.text: Ask a family code word, then pay without any other check.
choices.explanation: A word can leak or be overheard; it is an aid, not sole authorization.

questions.question: A CFO on a video call asks for an exceptional payment. Which step protects the decision?

choices.text: Verify the request through a known independent contact and required payment approvers.
choices.explanation: A separate transaction control survives a manipulated meeting or account.

choices.text: Message the same meeting chat for confirmation.
choices.explanation: The attacker may control that channel too.

choices.text: Pay if the face and voice have no artifacts.
choices.explanation: Quality is not authorization.

questions.question: An old friend unexpectedly messages you asking for money. Which check is strongest?

choices.text: Call the saved number or use another established route before deciding.
choices.explanation: A compromised account can know private message history.

choices.text: Ask a shared-memory question in the same chat and pay if answered.
choices.explanation: Chat history or public information may supply the answer.

choices.text: Run the message through an AI-text detector.
choices.explanation: Writing style detection does not establish account control or need.

questions.question: A viral clip has valid Content Credentials. What does that establish?

choices.text: A provenance record validates under its trust model; the clip’s claims still need corroboration.
choices.explanation: C2PA does not make truth judgments.

choices.text: The depicted claim must be true.
choices.explanation: Authentic provenance can accompany misleading content.

choices.text: Any clip without credentials must be fake.
choices.explanation: Legitimate media may lack credentials.

questions.question: A simple torch app asks for SMS, contacts and accessibility permissions. What is the best decision?

choices.text: Do not grant unrelated powerful permissions; verify the publisher and use a narrower alternative if needed.
choices.explanation: Permissions should fit function; accessibility capabilities vary by platform and setting.

choices.text: Grant them because app stores review all apps.
choices.explanation: Store review is not a reason for unrelated access.

choices.text: Assume every accessibility request means complete remote control.
choices.explanation: The exact powers vary, although this request is still excessive.

questions.question: Your phone loses service unexpectedly. You also receive an account-recovery notice. What is a proportionate first check?

choices.text: Use another trusted route to contact the carrier and affected service; check for a line or account change.
choices.explanation: A SIM takeover is possible, but an outage is also possible.

choices.text: Declare a confirmed SIM swap from “No service” alone.
choices.explanation: The observation does not establish the cause.

choices.text: Wait several days without checking.
choices.explanation: The recovery notice makes prompt low-risk checks appropriate.

questions.question: A browser extension wants access to all websites to perform a task needed on one site. What is the safer choice?

choices.text: Look for site-specific permission or a narrower alternative; verify the publisher before installing.
choices.explanation: A broad grant increases reach beyond the task.

choices.text: Grant all-sites access because legitimate extensions sometimes need it.
choices.explanation: Some do, but need and trust must be assessed for this task.

choices.text: Install it briefly; temporary use removes the risk.
choices.explanation: An extension can read data during that time.

questions.question: At a café, a bank page shows HTTPS. What does that tell you?

choices.text: The connection to that host is encrypted; verify the host and use a trusted entry route.
choices.explanation: Modern encrypted public Wi-Fi can be usable, while a scam site can also use HTTPS.

choices.text: The café Wi-Fi is always unsafe, even for encrypted sites.
choices.explanation: That blanket claim does not reflect modern HTTPS guidance.

choices.text: HTTPS proves the page belongs to your bank.
choices.explanation: Encryption does not prove business identity.

questions.question: A family sets filtering DNS on the home router. What limitation should they understand?

choices.text: It may block known domains for devices using that resolver, but cannot judge every scam or protect devices off that network.
choices.explanation: DNS filtering is a useful layer, not universal protection.

choices.text: It makes every device safe from any phishing attempt.
choices.explanation: Unknown domains, apps and alternate resolvers can bypass the layer.

choices.text: It guarantees protection while phones use mobile data.
choices.explanation: The home router does not control off-network traffic.

questions.question: You find an unfamiliar mail-forwarding rule after a login alert. What should you do?

choices.text: Treat it as a strong warning, verify it in the real account, remove unauthorized access and inspect recent activity.
choices.explanation: A forwarding rule may expose future mail; verify ownership before concluding.

choices.text: Assume the geographic login alert alone proves compromise.
choices.explanation: Travel and network routing can affect location labels.

choices.text: Ignore the rule because a login alert can be inaccurate.
choices.explanation: The rule itself needs investigation regardless of the alert.

questions.question: You cannot access email after a password-change alert. Which recovery path is sensible?

choices.text: Open the provider’s known recovery route on a device you trust; if the device may be compromised, use another trusted one.
choices.explanation: Incognito mode alone does not clean a compromised device.

choices.text: Use a link in the alert without checking its destination.
choices.explanation: The alert itself may be phishing.

choices.text: Assume an incognito window makes any infected device safe.
choices.explanation: Private browsing does not remove malware.

questions.question: An attacker is actively in your inbox right now. As an individual (not an organisation), what should you do?

choices.text: Quietly screenshot what they do for evidence.
choices.explanation: Watching an active intruder can prolong unauthorized access.

choices.text: Sign out all sessions, change the password, then capture the activity log.
choices.explanation: Use the genuine account or provider recovery route to change the secret, revoke sessions where supported, review forwarding/recovery settings, then preserve available activity records.

choices.text: Reply to one of their emails to confirm their identity.
choices.explanation: Replying may reveal more information without containing access.

choices.text: Set up DevTools monitoring on the inbox.
choices.explanation: Developer tools are not needed before basic account containment.

questions.question: A US resident discovers a new credit account opened in their name. Which response fits the situation?

choices.text: Contact the issuer, use IdentityTheft.gov for a tailored plan, and consider a freeze with the US credit bureaus.
choices.explanation: US-specific identity-theft tools help; reports and disputes depend on facts.

choices.text: Use the US credit-bureau process as universal advice in any country.
choices.explanation: Credit reporting and legal routes differ by jurisdiction.

choices.text: Wait for another account before acting.
choices.explanation: Delay can allow additional misuse.

questions.question: Three months after a credential-stuffing incident on your email, the single most useful follow-up action is:

choices.text: Create a new email and migrate everything.
choices.explanation: A new address alone does not remove old unauthorized access.

choices.text: Re-audit the email's security settings: active sessions, forwarding rules, OAuth apps, recovery contacts, login history.
choices.explanation: Review sessions, forwarding, third-party app access, recovery details and available login history to catch lingering unauthorized settings; not every past incident leaves one.

choices.text: Buy identity-theft insurance.
choices.explanation: Insurance does not inspect account settings.

choices.text: Reinstall the OS on all your devices.
choices.explanation: Reinstalling all devices is disproportionate without device-compromise evidence.
